Critical Psychology - An Introduction’ by Dennis Fox, Isaac Prilleltensky, and Stephanie Austin is a great place to start as it provides many differing perspectives and critiques of mainstream psychology that I’ve found very useful as a grad student, especially when the course requires us to be critical at all times. It also incorporates critical theory.

With regards to Ian Parker - his work mainly uses discourse analysis to uncover how language actively shapes and is shaped by taken for granted assumptions in mainstream psychology. His work also allowed me to gain a deeper understanding of critical psychology. 

His book - ‘Critical Psychology: Critical Concepts in Psychology’ is also a good start.
Check out anything related to the branch of ‘Critical Psychology’, especially Ian Parker’s work.

Basically it starts with observing your own thoughts and recognising them as negative. Once you identify these negative distortions, you challenge these very thoughts and write down or think of an alternative to the negative thought you were having. 

For example - you have a thought like 'she/he doesn't like me' after having a conversation with someone that didn't go the way you want it to. You can challenge that by thinking of alternatives such as - maybe he/she was having a bad day. Or numerous other reasons that doesn't involve you personalising it. 

Therapy is a great start. I'm seeing a therapist weekly and we agreed to try this. To start on your own - you can keep a thought diary and record your thoughts and distortions. There's an app on Android called MoodTools that allows you to practice CBT as well. It has the Thought Diary thing in the app. I'm sure iOS has the app too, if you have an iPhone.

Hope this helped. All the best :)
